lesson.title: Who knows where you are?
lesson.subtitle: Location, apps and the permissions you allow

video.title: Who knows where you are?
video.format_note: Animated explainer for students aged 12–16, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Amina Bello — the student's form teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talking to the student)

scenes.visual: Ms Amina in a classroom holds a phone showing a map with a moving dot and a chat group's name above it.
scenes.animation: The dot moves along a street; a timer reads 3 days.
scenes.narration: A student once told me, “Nobody knows where I am.” Then we opened her chat app together. Her live location had been on for three days, shared with a whole group.

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the cyber track chip.
scenes.narration: Today: how your phone knows where you are, and how you decide who else does.

scenes.visual: A phone in the middle; a satellite above, a Wi-Fi router to one side, a mobile mast to the other, each sending a signal line.
scenes.animation: Signal lines draw in one at a time.
scenes.narration: Your phone finds itself in three ways. Satellites, through GPS, find you outdoors to within a few metres. Nearby Wi-Fi networks help indoors. And your mobile network always knows which masts your phone is near, even with location switched off.

scenes.visual: An app icon on a phone opens a request bubble; behind it a queue of bubbles: camera, microphone, contacts, photos.
scenes.narration: Apps can ask to use that location, and also your camera, microphone, contacts and photos. Each yes you give is called a permission. Some are needed: a map needs your location to show the way. Many are not.

scenes.visual: A clean card: a thumb hovering between Allow and Don't allow; a question mark above.
scenes.animation: The thumb moves to Don't allow.
scenes.narration: So here's the rule. Before you tap Allow, ask: does this app need it to do its job? If the answer is no, tap Don't allow, and the app will usually work just fine.

scenes.visual: A settings screen with three switches: While using the app, Approximate, Ask every time.
scenes.animation: Each switch flips as it is named.
scenes.narration: Your phone gives you finer choices too. Only while using the app, instead of all the time. Approximate location, instead of your exact spot. And ask every time, for things you rarely use.

scenes.visual: Ms Amina holds up a phone with a torch app asking for location and contacts.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A torch app asks for your location and your contacts. What do you allow?

scenes.visual: The 'neither' card gets the check badge; the torch beam lights up.
scenes.narration: Neither. A torch needs the light on the back of your phone, nothing more. An app that wants far more than it needs is a reason to delete it.

scenes.visual: A student walks home; a dot follows her on her mother's phone; a timer counts down to zero and the dot disappears.
scenes.animation: Timer counts down; the dot fades out.
scenes.narration: Live location is useful, because your family can see you got home safely. Share it with family or one trusted friend, never a big group. Set a time limit, like one hour. Then check that it really stopped.

scenes.visual: A photo of a house; the corner peels back to show a map pin hidden inside the file.
scenes.animation: The photo corner folds; the pin pops out.
scenes.narration: Photos can carry a secret too. Many phone cameras save where each photo was taken inside the file, and some apps pass it on. Turn off location in your camera settings, and think twice before posting your house or your street.

scenes.visual: Ms Amina shows a class group chat with a live location bubble still running after a party.
scenes.narration: Your turn. You shared live location with your class group for a party, and it's still on. Leave it, or stop it?

scenes.visual: The 'stop it' card gets the check badge, then four summary cards line up.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right.
scenes.narration: Stop it now, because a whole group shouldn't know where you are all day. Remember: ask if the app needs it, choose only while using, share live location with family for a set time, and check your photos.

scenes.visual: A student and her older brother look at the location settings on a shared family phone.
scenes.animation: Switches turn off one by one.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: open your phone's settings, find location, and see which apps can use it. Switch it off for any app that doesn't need it. If it's a family phone, do it together with the person who owns it.

checkpoints.prompt: A torch app asks for your location and your contacts. What do you allow?

options.text: Neither — a torch only needs the light

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a torch needs the light on your phone, nothing else. Asking for more is a warning sign.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a torch has no reason to know where you are or who your friends are. Allow neither.

checkpoints.prompt: You shared live location with your class group for a party, and it's still on. Leave it, or stop it?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a whole group shouldn't be able to follow you all day. Share live location with family, for a set time.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a big group means many phones, and some may be lost or shared. Stop it now.
